name: Locavore
description: Locavore in Ubud is Bali's most celebrated fine dining restaurant and one of Southeast Asia's most principled—a farm-to-table operation that sources every ingredient from within Indonesia and uses that constraint as a creative springboard rather than a limitation. Chefs Ray Adriansyah and Eelke Plasmeijer have built relationships with small Balinese farmers, coastal fishermen, and jungle foragers over more than a decade, assembling an ingredient palette of extraordinary diversity—Balinese pork from a single heritage breed farm, turmeric from the restaurant's own garden, clams from specific coastal villages—and presenting it in a tasting menu of inventive, flavour-driven courses that draw on Indonesian, Balinese, and European culinary traditions. Locavore has been ranked in Asia's 50 Best multiple times and regularly described as the best restaurant in Indonesia.
reviewSummary: Indonesia's most acclaimed restaurant and Asia's 50 Best member—Locavore's 100% locally sourced Balinese tasting menu is the most creative and honest expression of Indonesian ingredients available anywhere.

spotlight.title: Indonesia's Greatest Restaurant: Dining at Locavore in Ubud, Bali
spotlight.excerpt: Asia's 50 Best, 100% locally sourced, and set in the cultural heart of Bali—Locavore has made Indonesia's ingredients the basis for some of Southeast Asia's most exciting fine dining. Here's what it's really like.
spotlight.introduction: When chefs Ray Adriansyah and Eelke Plasmeijer opened Locavore in 2014 in the small Balinese town of Ubud, they made a commitment that would shape everything about the restaurant: they would use only ingredients from Indonesia. Not only Bali—the whole archipelago, with its 17,000 islands and extraordinary biodiversity—but nothing imported. No French butter, no Breton scallops, no Spanish olive oil. This was not merely a sustainability gesture; it was a philosophical statement about the depth and complexity of Indonesian ingredients, which had never been represented at the fine dining level in their own country. A decade later, with multiple Asia's 50 Best rankings and a full waiting list for months in advance, that commitment has been vindicated magnificently.

sections.heading: The Ingredient Philosophy: Indonesia as a Pantry
content: Indonesia is one of the world's most biodiverse countries: 17,000 islands spanning the equator, encompassing rainforest, ocean, volcanic highlands, and coastal wetlands. The ingredient palette available to Locavore is, in theory, almost unlimited. In practice, Adriansyah and Plasmeijer have spent ten years building direct relationships with the specific farmers, fishermen, and foragers who supply them—relationships that go far beyond commercial transactions.

A single supplier grows a heritage breed of Balinese long pig that is fed on the restaurant's vegetable trimmings and foraged jungle plants; its flavour is categorically different from commercial pork—nuttier, richer, more complex. Another supplier cultivates fifteen varieties of Balinese turmeric, each with a different intensity and fragrance profile. A coastal village provides daily clams from a specific bay where the mineral content of the water produces shellfish of exceptional sweetness. Each of these relationships is visible in the food.

sections.heading: The Tasting Menu: Indonesia Course by Course
content: The Locavore menu runs to eight to ten courses, each one focused on a specific Indonesian ingredient or regional culinary tradition. An early snack course might present a single local ingredient—say, a young coconut—in five or six simultaneous preparations: raw, fermented, charred, concentrated into a sauce, dehydrated into a chip. This approach is both educational and surprising: you learn how much complexity exists within a single ingredient.

A seafood course typically draws on the extraordinary variety of Indonesian coastal waters: fish and shellfish you may have never encountered, prepared with techniques that honour their particular qualities. A recent menu featured Balinese barramundi cooked over coconut shell charcoal, served with a broth made from seaweed harvested by the restaurant's diving team and a side of sambal that had been fermented for three months.

The meat course is usually built around the heritage breed pork—perhaps a slow-roasted shoulder with a Balinese spice paste (the basa gede used in traditional ceremonial cooking), served with young jackfruit prepared to resemble the textures you expect from a classic braised preparation. The parallels with European fine dining techniques are clear; the flavours are entirely Indonesian.

sections.heading: The Setting: Ubud as Context
content: Locavore is located in a simply designed two-storey space on Jalan Dewi Sita, one of Ubud's most pleasant walking streets. The dining room is elegant without being ostentatious—natural wood, organic textures, Balinese ceramics created specifically for the restaurant. Through the window, the lush greenery of central Bali is visible; the air carries the smell of frangipani and incense from a nearby temple.

This context matters. Eating food made entirely from Balinese and Indonesian ingredients in Bali, in a restaurant that exists in genuine relationship with its landscape and community, creates a coherence between setting and plate that is rare and moving. You feel, in a way that few restaurants achieve, that you are genuinely understanding a place through its food.

locations: Jalan Dewi Sita, Ubud, Bali 80571, Indonesia

menuHighlights.Seafood: Indonesian coastal fish and shellfish from direct relationships
menuHighlights.Heritage Meat: Balinese long pig with traditional spice pastes
menuHighlights.Dessert: Indonesian tropical fruit, palm sugar, local chocolate

tips: Book at least 4-6 weeks in advance — Locavore is consistently fully booked.
The NoMeat menu (vegetarian) is equally accomplished — specify when booking.
The Locavore Not Bar cocktail programme uses only Indonesian spirits and botanicals.
Allow 3 hours for the full tasting menu experience.
Dress is smart casual; Bali's casual culture extends to the restaurant.
Ubud is 1.5 hours from Kuta/Seminyak — stay a night to avoid the commute.
Visit the Ubud food market at dawn before your dinner reservation for context.
spotlight.finalVerdict: Locavore is one of the most convincing arguments in contemporary gastronomy for why local sourcing, when pursued with genuine intelligence and commitment, produces not merely ethical food but better food. Every course is a discovery; the overall meal is a comprehensive, pleasurable education in what Indonesia's extraordinary biodiversity tastes like. This is Bali's finest restaurant and one of Southeast Asia's essential culinary experiences.
spotlight.author: Bali Culinary Explorer

name: Mozaic Restaurant Gastronomique
description: Mozaic in Ubud has been Bali's premier fine dining restaurant since chef Chris Salans arrived from France in 2001 and transformed an open-air garden into one of Asia's most romantic dining destinations. The tasting menu changes monthly and combines classical French technique with Indonesian ingredients—the Balinese spice markets are Salans' equivalent of the French herb garden. Dining under the canopy of a tropical garden, surrounded by the sounds of Bali's night birds, is an experience unlike anything else in Asian fine dining.
reviewSummary: Bali's most romantic fine dining experience since 2001—Mozaic's tropical garden setting and French-Balinese tasting menu create an atmosphere that is impossible to replicate.

name: Merah Putih
description: Merah Putih (Indonesian for 'Red and White', the national flag) in Seminyak is Bali's most visually spectacular restaurant—a soaring bamboo and glass structure housing an open kitchen that produces contemporary Indonesian cuisine from across the archipelago's seventeen thousand islands. Chef Mandif Warokka has created a menu that functions as a culinary tour of Indonesia: Padang rendang, Javanese satay, Manado seafood from North Sulawesi, Papuan jungle ingredients. The setting—bamboo arching sixty feet overhead, a wine cellar visible through a glass floor—is Bali's most impressive.
reviewSummary: Bali's most spectacular restaurant design paired with a contemporary Indonesian menu that covers the entire archipelago—Merah Putih is unmissable in Seminyak.

name: Warung Ibu Oka
description: Babi guling—Balinese spit-roasted suckling pig with turmeric, galangal, lemongrass, and a dozen other spices—is the island's most celebrated dish, prepared for ceremonies and special occasions for centuries. Warung Ibu Oka in Ubud, made internationally famous by Anthony Bourdain's No Reservations visit, serves the finest version available to tourists: a plate of crackled, spiced skin; tender, aromatic meat; sausage; blood curry; and rice, all assembled in a precise portion that is simultaneously a complete meal and one of the world's great single-dish experiences.
reviewSummary: Bali's most famous babi guling—Ibu Oka's ceremonial suckling pig, made globally famous by Anthony Bourdain, is the island's most essential culinary experience.

name: Ku De Ta
description: Ku De Ta on Bali's Seminyak beach is the island's most enduring beachfront dining institution—a place where the sound of waves, the golden Bali sunset, and a contemporary Asian fusion menu converge in an experience that has defined Seminyak's social scene since 2000. The food ranges from excellent wood-fired pizzas and fresh seafood to creative Indonesian-inflected dishes; the cocktail programme is exceptional; and the sunset here—the Indian Ocean sky turning from gold to crimson while you sip a Ku De Ta Sunset cocktail—is one of Bali's most reliable pleasures.
reviewSummary: Bali's most iconic beachfront restaurant since 2000—Ku De Ta's sunset, ocean sound, and contemporary Asian menu are the quintessential Seminyak experience.

name: The River Café
description: Perched above the Campuhan river gorge in Ubud with uninterrupted views of palm trees and Balinese jungle, The River Café offers what may be the most beautiful setting in the island's food scene. The Indonesian and international menu is simple, honest, and very good—nasi goreng (fried rice), grilled snapper, fresh juices made from Bali's extraordinary tropical fruit—served at the pace of the Balinese countryside surrounding it. This is Ubud at its most peaceful and most beautiful.
reviewSummary: The most beautiful setting in Ubud—The River Café's gorge views and simple, excellent Indonesian food create Bali's most peaceful and atmospheric dining experience.

name: Cuca
description: Cuca at Jimbaran Bay is Bali's most exciting casual fine dining restaurant—a partnership between chef Kevin Cherkas and wine director Virginia Entizne that produces a constantly evolving tapas-style menu drawing on Indonesian ingredients through a European small-plates lens. The smoked tuna with coconut sambal, the Balinese pork belly with palm sugar glaze, and the best cocktail programme in southern Bali have made Cuca essential dining since it opened. The prices remain remarkably accessible for the quality on offer.
reviewSummary: Bali's most exciting value fine dining—Cuca's Indonesian-European tapas menu at Jimbaran Bay delivers remarkable quality at prices that seem almost too low.

name: Naughty Nuri's Warung
description: No list of Bali's most essential eating experiences is complete without Naughty Nuri's in Ubud—a legendary warung (small Indonesian restaurant) that has been grilling pork ribs over charcoal since 1995 and serving them with a house marinade that is guarded with considerable secrecy. The ribs are sticky, caramelised, and falling from the bone; the martinis, dispensed in enormous quantities from behind a chaotic bar, are Ubud's most irreverent and beloved. This is not fine dining. It is essential dining.
reviewSummary: Bali's most legendary warung since 1995—Naughty Nuri's charcoal-grilled pork ribs and giant martinis in Ubud are the island's most beloved and irreverent dining tradition.

name: Jimbaran Seafood Cafés
description: The beach cafés along Jimbaran Bay, where the day's catch is grilled over coconut shell charcoal and served at tables on the sand with the Indian Ocean stretching before you and the sun setting behind Bali's sea temple of Tanah Lot, offer one of Asia's most complete sensory dining experiences. The lobster, red snapper, tiger prawns, and squid are sourced from Jimbaran's dawn fish market hours before they reach your table; the grilling is simple and precisely done; the sauces—sweet soy, sambal, garlic—complement without dominating. This is Bali's most iconic dining ritual.
reviewSummary: Bali's most iconic dining experience—fresh seafood grilled over coconut charcoal on Jimbaran Bay at sunset, with the Indian Ocean as your backdrop.
